hints: Trace the journey of a glucose molecule in Fig. 8.1 - which side does it start on in the tubule lumen, and which side must it finish on near the blood plasma?
Remember that uptake from the filtrate uses sodium-linked cotransporters on the lumen side, while movement into the blood uses ATP-driven sodium-potassium pumps on the blood side.
walkthrough:
Picture The One-Way Flow**
Think of the cell as a gate between two worlds. On the left is the filtrate in the tubule lumen, full of useful glucose, amino acids and sodium ions that need rescuing. On the right is the blood plasma where they need to go. So entry happens on the left, exit happens on the right.

Place C And P On Opposite Sides**
Cotransporters do the entry job, so C belongs on the highly folded left membrane - the microvilli touching the lumen. Sodium-potassium pumps do the exit job using ATP, so P belongs on the folded right membrane - the basal membrane touching the capillary. Your label lines must actually touch the membrane, not point into empty space.
Final answer: C with label line to the microvilli on the membrane facing the lumen of the proximal convoluted tubule. P with label line to the basal membrane facing the blood plasma.

hints: Start with the left side of the cell in Fig. 8.1 - why would a membrane that needs to absorb a lot very quickly be folded into hundreds of tiny microvilli?
Link that large surface area to proteins - what type of membrane protein must sit there to bring sodium ions in together with glucose or amino acids?
Look at the black bar joining the two cells - if there are gaps between cells, fluid could leak through, so how is fluid forced to go through the selective cell membranes instead?
Think about energy - reabsorption against concentration gradients needs ATP, so which organelle must be present in large numbers and what does that ATP power?
Finish on the right side of the cell - how does folding of the basal membrane help to fit in more pumps that move sodium out toward the blood?
walkthrough:
Maximise Uptake From The Filtrate**
The lumen-facing membrane is folded into microvilli, sometimes called a brush border. That hugely increases surface area, so many more cotransporter and carrier proteins can fit in. More proteins means faster reabsorption of glucose, amino acids and ions.

Couple Sodium To Useful Solutes**
Those apical cotransporters carry sodium ions down their concentration gradient together with glucose or amino acids into the cell. This is secondary active transport - the sodium gradient set up elsewhere drives the uptake, so all the glucose and amino acids in the filtrate can be reclaimed.

Force Everything Through The Cells**
Cells are joined by tight junctions that seal the gaps between them. Nothing can slip between cells, so all reabsorbed substances must pass through the selective cell-surface membranes where transport proteins control what is taken back.

Supply ATP And Pump Sodium To Blood**
The cell contains many mitochondria to make lots of ATP by aerobic respiration. The ATP powers sodium-potassium pumps in the basal membrane, which actively transport sodium ions out of the cell into the tissue fluid and blood. The basal membrane is highly folded to hold many of these pumps, keeping intracellular sodium low so more sodium and solutes keep entering from the lumen.

Final answer: Microvilli give large surface area for many cotransporter proteins; cotransporters absorb sodium ions with glucose / amino acids by secondary active transport; tight junctions between cells ensure substances pass through cells; many mitochondria produce ATP for sodium-potassium pumps; folded basal membrane houses many sodium-potassium pumps to actively transport sodium ions into blood.

hints: Find the urea row in Table 8.1 and pick out just two numbers - the percentage in glomerular filtrate and the percentage in urine.
To find how many times larger one value is, think about which operation compares them by division and what the result rounds to as a whole number.
walkthrough:
Pick Out The Correct Pair**
From Table 8.1, urea is $0.03$% in glomerular filtrate and $2.00$% in urine. You compare urine with filtrate because filtrate is the starting fluid and urine is the final fluid. Water is reabsorbed and only some urea is reabsorbed, so its percentage rises.

Divide And Round**
Fold increase $= \frac{\text{urine}}{\text{filtrate}} = \frac{2.00}{0.03} = 66.66...$ To the nearest whole number this is $67$. So urea is about 67 times more concentrated as a percentage in urine than in filtrate.
